# Speedle AI — AI agent authorization and access control

> Speedle AI is the Speedle site for access management for AI. It shows how to apply the open-source Speedle policy engine to authorization for AI agents: MCP tool calls, permission-aware RAG, agent-to-agent (A2A) calls, zero standing privileges (ZSP) and the AI lifecycle from training data to model release. It also previews Speedle MCP for designing, managing and checking policies with AI, and an AI-based risk-detection approach that is being built. Everything here is a solution pattern on the Speedle policy engine; none of it is a shipped integration with an ML or agent platform.

Source: https://ai.speedle.io/

## What is Speedle AI?

Speedle AI has two connected directions.

- **AI for access management:** AI helping people design, manage and check access policies with the open-source Speedle policy modeler skill and Speedle MCP, plus an AI-based risk-detection approach being built.
- **Access management for AI:** policy patterns that govern what AI systems and agents may do while they are built and while they run.

Both directions rest on clear, enforceable policy decisions. Speedle decides; the application enforces the decision.

## AI for access management

### Speedle policy modeler skill

An open-source Agent Skill for Claude Code at `skills/speedle-policy-modeler/` in teramoby/ai.speedle.io. It reads a company regulation, employee handbook or access matrix; asks the document owner to clarify missing org structure, roles, resources, attributes, exceptions and approval chains in small prioritized batches; and writes an RBAC + ABAC model.

Outputs: `policies.spdl` in the Speedle file-store format, a `model.md` design document with a Mermaid role-inheritance diagram and a rationale for every policy, a `test-cases.json` suite, and `results.md`. The skill refuses to guess an authorization rule; every policy cites a handbook clause or a confirmed answer.

Example runs: English and Chinese synthetic handbooks. Both pass `spctl check` and 37 of 37 authorization cases against a local PMS and ADS. The SPDL uses exact or prefix resource expressions only, so the evaluator uses hash-map and radix-tree lookups.

Install: copy `skills/speedle-policy-modeler/` to `~/.claude/skills/` for a personal skill or `.claude/skills/` for a project skill, then run `/speedle-policy-modeler ./employee-handbook.md`. The `SKILL.md` frontmatter follows the Agent Skills format with `name` and `description`.

- Skill folder: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/tree/main/skills/speedle-policy-modeler
- English sample: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/blob/main/skills/speedle-policy-modeler/examples/en/model.md
- Chinese sample: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/blob/main/skills/speedle-policy-modeler/examples/zh/model.md

### Speedle MCP (launch preview)

`@speedle/mcp` is planned as one npm package with a `speedle-mcp` binary that runs as a local stdio MCP server. It is an MCP server for authorization work, with two deliberately separate modes. It is not published on npm yet.

- **check mode:** registers only `is_allowed` by default and reads only ADS configuration. `diagnose`, `all_granted_roles` and `all_granted_permissions` are opt-in through the `--expose-diagnose`, `--expose-all-granted-roles` and `--expose-all-granted-permissions` flags (or the matching `SPEEDLE_EXPOSE_*` environment variables). `diagnose` works only with self-hosted Speedle; the server will not start with it against Speedle Cloud. It answers authorization questions through the Speedle ADS REST API using subject, resource, action and typed attributes; it does not enforce anything in the calling application.
- **manage mode:** registers only the management tools and reads only PMS configuration for designing and managing Speedle policies through the PMS REST API: services, authorization policies, role policies, SPDL validation and effective-policy explanation helpers. A read-only option exists and destructive deletes require explicit target confirmation.

Security rule: never give the manage mode to an agent that is itself governed by these policies. An agent holding both check and management tools could be prompted into granting itself access. Give a governed agent `is_allowed` only, which is the check-mode default: `diagnose`, `all_granted_roles` and `all_granted_permissions` show policies, conditions and grants, so turn them on only in a check server for policy authors and operators, and never pass the `--expose-*` flags to the agent's server. There is no default mode that exposes both; running with no mode is planned to print usage and exit non-zero.

Install and MCP client configuration snippets on the site are future launch examples, marked "Available at launch". They do not work today.

### AI-based risk detection (being built)

AI-based risk detection is a direction Speedle is exploring and building, not a shipped feature. The approach looks across more dimensions and relationships than a single rule, for example unusual combinations of agent, user, data and task context.

Policy keeps the veto. The target flow is: request context, then the deterministic policy decision, then AI risk signals, then a final decision. A policy deny stops at the decision step; risk signals can add scrutiny or protection but can never turn a policy deny into an allow.

## Access management for AI

Speedle's policy engine applied wherever AI systems touch data, models, tools and other agents. Each area has an enforcement point in the application; it asks Speedle before it acts and enforces the answer. Identity comes in from the IdP; decisions and explanations go out to the audit trail. The SPDL examples below are solution patterns, not shipped platform integrations.

### Build: data and training

Training jobs read datasets, use compute and write checkpoints. The application asks before each dataset read, job start and checkpoint export, passing sensitivity, tenant, consent and region as attributes.

- Subjects: training pipelines as entities; ML engineers and their teams.
- Resources and actions: datasets `read`, training jobs `start`, checkpoints `export`.
- Enforcement point: the data loader before it opens a dataset, the job scheduler before it allocates compute, and the artifact store before an export.
- SPDL example rules: consent and region checked per dataset, restricted data denied outright, and a GPU-hour limit on job start.

### Build: model release

Registering, approving, promoting and rolling back models are separate actions with separate owners. Separation of duties keeps the person who trained a model from approving it.

- Subjects: ML engineers, release managers and the service identities of release pipelines.
- Resources and actions: models and endpoints with `register`, `approve`, `promote` and `rollback`.
- Enforcement point: the model registry and the release pipeline, before each change of model or endpoint state.

### Run: inference and permission-aware RAG

Users, apps and tenants call models. For permission-aware RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), the retriever asks Speedle about each document or collection before its content enters the prompt, so the model only sees what the person behind the request may read.

- Subjects: the user behind the request with their groups; client applications and tenants as entities.
- Resources and actions: collections and documents `retrieve`; models `invoke`.
- Enforcement point: the retriever before a document enters the prompt, and the API gateway or inference service before it routes a request.
- SPDL example rules: a document is retrieved only inside the user's tenant and at a label the user is cleared for; legal-hold documents are denied; apps call only the model tiers in their plan.

### Run: agents acting for users

The agent has its own identity, and the user's delegation is proven by a signed delegation token, not by claims in the request. The enforcement point verifies the token, then asks Speedle twice and allows only if both checks pass: the agent within the token's scope, and the delegating user with their own permissions now. If the user loses a permission after the token was issued, the agent loses it at the next request. A refund above 100 also needs a recorded human approval by someone other than the user.

1. Verify the token: signature, issuer, expiry, and that it was issued to this agent.
2. Agent scope: ask Speedle with the agent as subject and the token's scope as attributes.
3. Delegator now: ask Speedle with the delegating user, named by the token's `sub` claim, as subject.

- Subjects: the agent as an entity for the scope check; the delegating user, taken from the verified token, for the second check.
- Resources and actions: tickets `read` and `update`; orders `refund`, with the amount as an attribute. All limited to the actions and resources in the token's scope.
- Enforcement point: the agent runtime or the application backend before the action reaches the business system. It verifies the token and passes only verified claims to Speedle.
- Human approval: the enforcement point verifies the signed approval record for the refund and passes its approver as `approved_by` in the second check. The approver must not be the user.
- Self-hosted option: one check, with the token and the delegator evaluated by the custom functions `DelegationValid` and `DelegatorAllowed`. Speedle Cloud does not run custom functions.
- SPDL example rules: the agent gets its role in three steps (token not expired, action listed, resource listed), so it holds only within the token's scope; the delegator's grants ask about the user alone, so revoking the user's role denies the agent at the next request; a refund above 100 is granted only with an approver other than the user.

A runnable local sample of both patterns, with a demo token issuer, the enforcement point and the custom-function server, is in the repository: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/tree/main/samples/delegation

### Run: tool calls over MCP

Every tool call is checked before it runs. The tool is the resource, the call is the action, and the arguments become attributes, so limits such as a refund amount are part of the policy.

- Subjects: agents, each with its own entity identity and role, so privileges stay per agent and per tool.
- Resources and actions: tools `call`, with the tool arguments as attributes.
- Enforcement point: the MCP client host, or a gateway in front of MCP servers, before the tool executes.

### Run: agent-to-agent (A2A) authorization

Each hop in a delegation chain is checked. The callee may receive only scopes the caller already holds, and the chain has a hop limit, so delegation only narrows permissions.

- Subjects: calling agents, identified as entities.
- Resources and actions: other agents and their skills `call`, with the requested scopes, the caller's scopes and the hop count as attributes.
- Enforcement point: the calling agent before it sends a task, or the receiving agent before it accepts one.

### Run: zero standing privileges (ZSP)

Just-in-time, short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials can support a zero standing privileges (ZSP) pattern when token issuance and other controls are in place. On self-hosted Speedle Engine, the policy checks a positive and short lifetime, that the token is not issued or valid in the future beyond a 60-second clock-skew allowance, that it has not expired, and, through a read-only custom function, that it is unused in the issuer's store. (Speedle Cloud does not support custom external functions.) The application or enforcement layer then consumes a single-use token atomically before the operation; production also verifies the token's signature, issuer, audience and binding before its claims reach the policy.

A runnable local sample with PMS, ADS and the custom function, including the atomic consume step, is in the repository: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/tree/main/samples/zsp

### Cross-cutting concerns

- **Identity integration:** Speedle is the authorization decision point. Authentication comes from the IdP or OAuth authorization server, for users and for agents; MCP authorization builds on OAuth. The application maps verified identities to principals and Speedle decides on the principals it is given.
- **Audit and explainability:** Speedle's diagnose API returns the decision, the reason, the effective roles and the policies examined, including which one matched and why. Applications log each decision with the agent and the delegating human. Diagnose exposes policy and request details, so keep it to trusted operators.
- **Risk mapping:** the patterns map to OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency: an agent with more functionality, permission or autonomy than its task needs. Per-agent roles, per-tool checks, task- and time-bound delegation and human approval for high-risk actions narrow each of the three.

### Where Speedle stops

Speedle does not detect prompt injection, filter model input or output, or verify model and dataset supply chains; use dedicated controls for those. It bounds what a compromised or misled agent can do: Speedle answers deny to any request outside policy, whatever the prompt said.
